## agent-ml-research
ML research experiment management tools

attachment.content:
- update-config: Use this skill to configure the Claude Code harness via settings.json. Automated behaviors ("from now on when X", "each time X", "whenever X", "before/after X") require hooks configured in settings.json - the harness executes these, not Claude, so memory/preferences cannot fulfill them. Also use for: permissions ("allow X", "add permission", "move permission to"), env vars ("set X=Y"), hook troubleshooting, or any changes to settings.json/settings.local.json files. Examples: "allow npm commands", "add bq permission to global settings", "move permission to user settings", "set DEBUG=true", "when claude stops show X". For simple settings like theme/model, suggest the /config command.
- keybindings-help: Use when the user wants to customize keyboard shortcuts, rebind keys, add chord bindings, or modify ~/.claude/keybindings.json. Examples: "rebind ctrl+s", "add a chord shortcut", "change the submit key", "customize keybindings".
- simplify: Review changed code for reuse, quality, and efficiency, then fix any issues found.
- fewer-permission-prompts: Scan your transcripts for common read-only Bash and MCP tool calls, then add a prioritized allowlist to project .claude/settings.json to reduce permission prompts.
- loop: Run a prompt or slash command on a recurring interval (e.g. /loop 5m /foo). Omit the interval to let the model self-pace. - When the user wants to set up a recurring task, poll for status, or run something repeatedly on an interval (e.g. "check the deploy every 5 minutes", "keep running /babysit-prs"). Do NOT invoke for one-off tasks.
- schedule: Create, update, list, or run scheduled remote agents (routines) that execute on a cron schedule. - When the user wants to schedule a recurring remote agent, set up automated tasks, create a cron job for Claude Code, or manage their scheduled agents/routines. Also use when the user wants a one-time scheduled run ("run this once at 3pm", "remind me to check X tomorrow").
- claude-api: Build, debug, and optimize Claude API / Anthropic SDK apps. Apps built with this skill should include prompt caching. Also handles migrating existing Claude API code between Claude model versions (4.5 → 4.6, 4.6 → 4.7, retired-model replacements).
TRIGGER when: code imports `anthropic`/`@anthropic-ai/sdk`; user asks for the Claude API, Anthropic SDK, or Managed Agents; user adds/modifies/tunes a Claude feature (caching, thinking, compaction, tool use, batch, files, citations, memory) or model (Opus/Sonnet/Haiku) in a file; questions about prompt caching / cache hit rate in an Anthropic SDK project.
SKIP: file imports `openai`/other-provider SDK, filename like `*-openai.py`/`*-generic.py`, provider-neutral code, general programming/ML.
- init: Initialize a new CLAUDE.md file with codebase documentation
- review: Review a pull request
- security-review: Complete a security review of the pending changes on the current branch

14	When $S(t) \cap G(t) = \emptyset$---tight constraints leave no token that is both grammar-valid and semantically valid---na\"{\i}ve masking would force selection of a grammar-invalid token, breaking JSON structure.

% Section: Constraint Composition (compressed, 787→~500 words)

At each decoding step $t$, let $G(t) \subseteq V$ and $S(t) \subseteq V$ denote the tokens permitted by the grammar and semantic layers, respectively.
The final mask is their conjunction:
%
\begin{equation}\label{eq:composition}
  M_{\text{final}}(t) = M_{\text{grammar}}(t) \;\wedge\; M_{\text{semantic}}(t),
\end{equation}
%
so a token is allowed only if it satisfies \emph{both} structural and type-level constraints.
The conjunction is asymmetric: $S(t)$ is defined only over $G(t)$, reflecting the enabling dependency (\S\ref{sec:method})---the semantic layer requires the relation type to belong to $\mathcal{R}$, a property guaranteed only by the grammar layer.

\paragraph{Grammar-First Fallback.}
When $S(t) \cap G(t) = \emptyset$---tight constraints leave no token that is both grammar-valid and semantically valid---na\"{\i}ve masking would force selection of a grammar-invalid token, breaking JSON structure.
We enforce a \emph{grammar-first fallback}: if no semantically valid token survives grammar filtering, semantic masking is skipped and the grammar layer alone controls selection.
Structural integrity is a hard constraint; a type violation is a soft error detectable by downstream validation.

\paragraph{Constraint Tightness.}
We define the tightness of relation $r$ as:
%
\begin{equation}\label{eq:tightness}
  \tau(r) = 1 - \frac{|\mathcal{V}(r)|}{|\mathcal{T}|^2},
\end{equation}
%
where $\mathcal{V}(r)$ is the set of valid type pairs and $\mathcal{T}$ the entity type vocabulary.
The mean tightness $\bar{\tau} = \frac{1}{|\mathcal{R}|}\sum_{r} \tau(r)$ characterizes ontology restrictiveness.
Tighter constraints eliminate more grammar-valid tokens at type-bearing positions, increasing fallback frequency and residual DR.
This dual-factor mechanism---tightness $\times$ baseline model violation rate---explains the cross-dataset pattern: SciERC ($\bar{\tau}{=}0.333$, 24 valid pairs/relation) achieves 94--99\% DR reduction, while DocRED ($\bar{\tau}{=}0.842$, 5.68 pairs) achieves 45--90\%, with the residual modulated by model-specific baselines (\S\ref{sec:cross-model}).

\paragraph{Decidability Taxonomy.}
We classify ontology constraints by when sufficient information becomes available:
%
\begin{enumerate}[leftmargin=*,nosep]
  \item \textbf{Local}: require only the current token (entity/relation vocabulary membership). Handled by the grammar layer.
  \item \textbf{Prefix-decidable}: require the decoded prefix (domain/range constraints). Handled by the semantic layer via the entity registry.
  \item \textbf{Non-local}: require information not yet generated (forward coreference). Outside the scope of single-pass decoding; partially addressed by the two-pass strategy (S2, \S\ref{sec:s2}).
\end{enumerate}

6	---
7	
8	## Summary of the Paper
9	
10	This paper identifies that LLM-based zero-shot information extraction produces systematic ontology constraint violations (15-19% of triples violate domain/range rules on SciERC and DocRED), conducts a per-relation violation landscape study showing that violation rates correlate with constraint tightness rather than ontology size, and proposes OntoCoDec -- a two-layer constrained decoding framework that compiles IE ontology schemas into a grammar layer (XGrammar CFG for structural/vocabulary validity) and a semantic layer (stateful entity registry + dynamic logit masking for domain/range enforcement). On SciERC the system achieves 94% DR reduction at zero F1 cost; on DocRED, 45-90% DR reduction depending on the model, with cross-model validation on Qwen3-8B and Llama-3.1-8B.
11	
12	## Summary of Strengths
13	
14	- S1: **The violation landscape study is a genuine empirical contribution.** No prior work has systematically measured per-relation ontology constraint violation distributions in LLM-based IE. The finding that comparable DR rates emerge across ontologies differing 14x in size (SciERC 15.4% vs DocRED 18.5%), with the key predictor being constraint tightness rather than ontology scale, is non-obvious and practically useful. The Evaluate-for regression (+5.8pp under schema-informed prompting) provides concrete evidence that prompt-level intervention is not merely insufficient but can be counterproductive.
15	
16	- S2: **Thorough and honestly reported experimental design.** The 4/5-way ablation cleanly isolates each layer's contribution, with cross-model (2x2 matrix), post-hoc filtering baseline, bootstrap CIs (10,000 iterations), and per-relation breakdowns. Negative results are transparently disclosed: CF elevation to 9.90%, grammar-only DR *increase* on DocRED, S2 null result, post-hoc filtering achieving higher F1. This level of honesty strengthens the paper's credibility.
17	
18	- S3: **The related work section is substantially more thorough than the original brief submission context suggested.** Six organized paradigms with ~42 references. The PICARD/Synchromesh/PLDI'25 differentiation is technically precise, and the paper correctly identifies the key IE-specific challenge (entity registry populated during generation from free text, vs. fixed schema in SQL/code). The concurrent work coverage (OntoLogX, Zhou et al. 2026 ontology-to-tools) is commendable.
19	
20	- S4: **The dual-factor model (tightness x model RV baseline) for DR reduction is analytically stronger than a naive single-factor story.** Qwen's 29.66% RV baseline causing grammar enforcement to surface latent DR violations, yielding only 45% DR reduction on the same ontology where Llama (RV 16.03%) achieves 90.2%, is a genuine insight about model-constraint interaction.
21	
22	- S5: **Post-hoc filtering comparison is well-framed.** Rather than competing on F1 (where post-hoc wins by removing FPs in a low-F1 regime), the paper correctly argues along multiple dimensions: recall preservation, TP retention (127 lost on DocRED), entity-type violation persistence (post-hoc ET=2.47% vs OntoCoDec ET=0%), and streaming compatibility.
23	
24	## Summary of Weaknesses
25	
26	- W1: [Major] **Core technical contribution has limited novelty.** The paper's central technical mechanism -- compiling ontological type constraints into token-level logit masks applied during autoregressive decoding -- is a domain transfer of techniques well-established in the code generation literature to a *structurally simpler* constraint system. PICARD (EMNLP 2021) maintains incremental parsing state for SQL type checking. Synchromesh (ICLR 2022) enforces type and scope constraints via dynamic token masks. The PLDI 2025 work compiles full type systems (with subtyping and parametric polymorphism) into prefix automata for logit masking. IE ontology constraints -- flat domain/range sets over 6 entity types -- are dramatically simpler than these systems. The entity registry is a dictionary lookup; the composition mechanism is standard bitwise AND. The paper acknowledges the code-gen parallel but does not convincingly articulate what IE-specific technical challenge required a solution *beyond* what these systems already provide. The free-text entity span argument (entities discovered during generation, not declared upfront) is valid but the actual implementation (building a dict as entities are parsed) is straightforward.
27	
28	- W2: [Major] **The decidability taxonomy is not a meaningful contribution.** The local / prefix-decidable / non-local classification follows directly from basic properties of left-to-right autoregressive generation. That entity-type membership is locally decidable, domain/range constraints are prefix-decidable once the registry is built, and forward coreference is non-local -- these are obvious consequences of the generation order. Similar (and more rigorous) taxonomies appear implicitly in Synchromesh, MGD, and the PLDI 2025 work. Presenting this as a contribution (it appears in the abstract and is repeated in multiple sections) inflates the paper's novelty claims. It would be better positioned as design rationale or organizational framework.
29	
30	- W3: [Major] **DocRED results are weak and strain the "near-complete" framing.** For Qwen3-8B on DocRED, DR drops only from 18.46% to 10.21% -- a 45% reduction, leaving more than 1 in 10 triples with domain/range violations. One of four cells in the 2x2 evaluation matrix retains >10% violation rate. The title "Near-Complete Type-Valid Information Extraction" is defensible for SciERC (0.93%) and Llama-DocRED (2.55%) but misleading for Qwen-DocRED. The paper should either qualify "near-complete" more carefully or acknowledge that the system's effectiveness is highly dependent on the interaction between model RV baseline and ontology tightness.
31	
32	- W4: [Moderate] **CF trade-off is substantial and the severity distinction is asserted, not validated.** CF rises from 0.08% to 9.90% on SciERC (Qwen) and to 12.02% on DocRED (Llama). The paper frames DR as "hard" and CF as "soft" violations, arguing that individual triples remain type-valid under CF. This distinction is plausible but entirely unvalidated: no downstream evaluation shows that CF violations are indeed less harmful. The dominant conflict pattern (Generic <-> OtherScientificTerm) is attributed to type system ambiguity, which risks dismissing a method limitation as a dataset artifact. Ablation evidence cleanly attributes CF to the semantic layer (grammar-only CF=0.08%), which is informative but does not reduce the practical impact.
33	
34	- W5: [Moderate] **Evaluation scope is narrow for the generality of claims.** Two 8B-class models, two datasets, zero-shot only, R-F1 of 2-8%. ## Summary of the Paper

This paper identifies that LLM-based zero-shot information extraction produces systematic ontology constraint violations (15-19% of triples violate domain/range rules on SciERC and DocRED), conducts a per-relation violation landscape study showing that violation rates correlate with constraint tightness rather than ontology size, and proposes OntoCoDec -- a two-layer constrained decoding framework that compiles IE ontology schemas into a grammar layer (XGrammar CFG for structural/vocabulary validity) and a semantic layer (stateful entity registry + dynamic logit masking for domain/range enforcement). On SciERC the system achieves 94% DR reduction at zero F1 cost; on DocRED, 45-90% DR reduction depending on the model, with cross-model validation on Qwen3-8B and Llama-3.1-8B.

## Summary of Strengths

- S1: **The violation landscape study is a genuine empirical contribution.** No prior work has systematically measured per-relation ontology constraint violation distributions in LLM-based IE. The finding that comparable DR rates emerge across ontologies differing 14x in size (SciERC 15.4% vs DocRED 18.5%), with the key predictor being constraint tightness rather than ontology scale, is non-obvious and practically useful. The Evaluate-for regression (+5.8pp under schema-informed prompting) provides concrete evidence that prompt-level intervention is not merely insufficient but can be counterproductive.

- S2: **Thorough and honestly reported experimental design.** The 4/5-way ablation cleanly isolates each layer's contribution, with cross-model (2x2 matrix), post-hoc filtering baseline, bootstrap CIs (10,000 iterations), and per-relation breakdowns. Negative results are transparently disclosed: CF elevation to 9.90%, grammar-only DR *increase* on DocRED, S2 null result, post-hoc filtering achieving higher F1. This level of honesty strengthens the paper's credibility.

- S3: **The related work section is substantially more thorough than the original brief submission context suggested.** Six organized paradigms with ~42 references. The PICARD/Synchromesh/PLDI'25 differentiation is technically precise, and the paper correctly identifies the key IE-specific challenge (entity registry populated during generation from free text, vs. fixed schema in SQL/code). The concurrent work coverage (OntoLogX, Zhou et al. 2026 ontology-to-tools) is commendable.

- S4: **The dual-factor model (tightness x model RV baseline) for DR reduction is analytically stronger than a naive single-factor story.** Qwen's 29.66% RV baseline causing grammar enforcement to surface latent DR violations, yielding only 45% DR reduction on the same ontology where Llama (RV 16.03%) achieves 90.2%, is a genuine insight about model-constraint interaction.

- S5: **Post-hoc filtering comparison is well-framed.** Rather than competing on F1 (where post-hoc wins by removing FPs in a low-F1 regime), the paper correctly argues along multiple dimensions: recall preservation, TP retention (127 lost on DocRED), entity-type violation persistence (post-hoc ET=2.47% vs OntoCoDec ET=0%), and streaming compatibility.

## Summary of Weaknesses

- W1: [Major] **Core technical contribution has limited novelty.** The paper's central technical mechanism -- compiling ontological type constraints into token-level logit masks applied during autoregressive decoding -- is a domain transfer of techniques well-established in the code generation literature to a *structurally simpler* constraint system. PICARD (EMNLP 2021) maintains incremental parsing state for SQL type checking. Synchromesh (ICLR 2022) enforces type and scope constraints via dynamic token masks. The PLDI 2025 work compiles full type systems (with subtyping and parametric polymorphism) into prefix automata for logit masking. IE ontology constraints -- flat domain/range sets over 6 entity types -- are dramatically simpler than these systems. The entity registry is a dictionary lookup; the composition mechanism is standard bitwise AND. The paper acknowledges the code-gen parallel but does not convincingly articulate what IE-specific technical challenge required a solution *beyond* what these systems already provide. The free-text entity span argument (entities discovered during generation, not declared upfront) is valid but the actual implementation (building a dict as entities are parsed) is straightforward.

- W2: [Major] **The decidability taxonomy is not a meaningful contribution.** The local / prefix-decidable / non-local classification follows directly from basic properties of left-to-right autoregressive generation. That entity-type membership is locally decidable, domain/range constraints are prefix-decidable once the registry is built, and forward coreference is non-local -- these are obvious consequences of the generation order. Similar (and more rigorous) taxonomies appear implicitly in Synchromesh, MGD, and the PLDI 2025 work. Presenting this as a contribution (it appears in the abstract and is repeated in multiple sections) inflates the paper's novelty claims. It would be better positioned as design rationale or organizational framework.

- W3: [Major] **DocRED results are weak and strain the "near-complete" framing.** For Qwen3-8B on DocRED, DR drops only from 18.46% to 10.21% -- a 45% reduction, leaving more than 1 in 10 triples with domain/range violations. One of four cells in the 2x2 evaluation matrix retains >10% violation rate. The title "Near-Complete Type-Valid Information Extraction" is defensible for SciERC (0.93%) and Llama-DocRED (2.55%) but misleading for Qwen-DocRED. The paper should either qualify "near-complete" more carefully or acknowledge that the system's effectiveness is highly dependent on the interaction between model RV baseline and ontology tightness.

- W4: [Moderate] **CF trade-off is substantial and the severity distinction is asserted, not validated.** CF rises from 0.08% to 9.90% on SciERC (Qwen) and to 12.02% on DocRED (Llama). The paper frames DR as "hard" and CF as "soft" violations, arguing that individual triples remain type-valid under CF. This distinction is plausible but entirely unvalidated: no downstream evaluation shows that CF violations are indeed less harmful. The dominant conflict pattern (Generic <-> OtherScientificTerm) is attributed to type system ambiguity, which risks dismissing a method limitation as a dataset artifact. Ablation evidence cleanly attributes CF to the semantic layer (grammar-only CF=0.08%), which is informative but does not reduce the practical impact.

- W5: [Moderate] **Evaluation scope is narrow for the generality of claims.** Two 8B-class models, two datasets, zero-shot only, R-F1 of 2-8%. No fine-tuned model, no larger model, no domain beyond scientific/Wikipedia text. The claim "model-agnostic generalization" in the introduction and cross-model section overreaches from a 2-model sample. More critically, the practical motivation for constraint enforcement is arguably strongest in the fine-tuned regime where F1 is meaningful and residual violations matter for downstream applications -- yet this regime is entirely unexamined.

The claim as stated may be technically correct but is stronger than warranted without acknowledging these adjacent literatures.

The 24% vs 94% gap is empirically informative, but framing this as a key finding rather than a design requirement inflates its significance.

DocRED with 96 relations would provide much stronger evidence, but per-relation DR under constrained decoding is not reported for DocRED at the same granularity.

- Q1: What specific IE technical challenge does OntoCoDec solve that the PLDI'25 type-constrained code generation system (or a straightforward adaptation of it) cannot? Beyond the entity registry being populated during generation -- which is a dict lookup -- what is the algorithmic innovation?

- Q2: The fallback rate on DocRED (10.2%, 1770/17341 triples) and residual DR (10.21%) are nearly identical. If the former, the "tightness predicts DR" chain is partially circular -- tightness causes fallback, fallback *is* residual DR, therefore tightness "predicts" DR.

- Q3: Have you measured or estimated violation rates in a fine-tuned IE system? If fine-tuned models on SciERC already achieve <2% DR, the practical motivation for decoding-time enforcement narrows substantially. Conversely, if fine-tuned models retain non-trivial DR, that would greatly strengthen the paper.

- Q4: The semantic-only configuration on DocRED *increases* ET violations (2.48% -> 4.22%). This negative interaction effect -- partial constraint application worsening a different violation category -- seems concerning and underexplored. What is the mechanism, and does it carry implications for deploying individual constraint layers?

- Q5: How does the system handle entities that appear in relations but were not present in the entity list? The registry lookup would fail. What fraction of triples contain entities absent from the entity list, and how does this affect DR enforcement?

## Missing References

The related work is substantially more complete than initially apparent (~42 references across 6 paradigms). However, several notable gaps remain:

1. **SynCode (Ugare et al., 2024)** -- Grammar-constrained decoding with semantic validation for Python/Go, directly relevant to the grammar+semantic layering.
2. **TANL (Paolini et al., ICLR 2021)** -- Translation-based IE that frames extraction as augmented natural language generation; relevant as a training-based structured generation baseline.
3. **REBEL (Cabot & Navigli, EMNLP 2021)** -- Autoregressive relation extraction with constrained beam search over relation triples.
4. **Neuro-symbolic constraint literature** -- DeepProbLog (Manhaeve et al., NeurIPS 2018), Semantic Loss (Xu et al., ICML 2018), posterior regularization (Ganchev et al., JMLR 2010). OntoCoDec's approach of compiling declarative constraints into procedural enforcement is a specific instance of this broader research direction. This connection is entirely absent.
5. **KG embedding type constraints** -- TransR (Lin et al., AAAI 2015), type-constrained negative sampling (Krompass et al., 2015). These enforce type constraints in representation learning and motivate why type validity matters for KG applications.
6. **Schema-guided dialogue** -- SGD (Rastogi et al., AAAI 2020) and related work on schema-following constrained generation in task-oriented dialogue, which shares the "compile schema into generation constraints" paradigm.
7. **InstructUIE (Wang et al., 2023)** -- Mentioned in the summary context but not cited in the actual paper; zero-shot IE with instruction tuning.

## Venue Calibration

EMNLP 2026 submissions go through ACL Rolling Review. Scoring uses a 1–5 scale with half-point increments:
- 5 = Award-worthy (top 2.5%)
- 4 = Largely complete, minor revisions
- 3 = Major revisions needed
- 2 = Significant revisions / resubmit next cycle
- 1.5 = Resubmit after next cycle
- 1 = Not publishable at *ACL

Three dimensions scored: Soundness, Excitement, Overall Assessment. EMNLP 2025 acceptance rate was ~26% for main conference.

---

## Paper Summary

The paper addresses ontology constraint violations in LLM-based zero-shot information extraction. It makes two main contributions: (1) a **violation landscape study** measuring domain/range (DR), relation vocabulary (RV), entity type (ET), and cross-field consistency (CF) violations on SciERC (7 relations) and DocRED (96 relations); (2) **OntoCoDec**, a framework that compiles IE ontology schemas into two composable constrained-decoding layers — a grammar layer (XGrammar CFG for JSON/vocabulary enforcement) and a semantic layer (stateful entity registry + dynamic logit masking for domain/range constraints). On SciERC, DR violations drop 94% (15.4%→0.93%) with neutral F1; on DocRED, 45% (Qwen) to 90% (Llama). The method introduces cross-field consistency violations (2.6–12.0%) as a trade-off.

---

## Experiment Coverage Assessment

The paper covers experiments P001–P016 and P018–P019 from the full experiment plan. P017 (50-doc pilot) was superseded by the full S2 evaluation. P020 was killed/superseded. All major planned experiments are reported. The paper's experimental matrix (2 models × 2 datasets × 5 configurations + post-hoc baseline + bootstrap CI) is comprehensive for the claims made.

---

## Reviewer 1 (R1): Methods and Experiments

### Strengths

**S1: Violation landscape study is a genuine empirical contribution.** No prior work systematically quantifies per-relation ontology constraint violation distributions in LLM-based IE. The finding that SciERC (7 relations, DR=15.4%) and DocRED (96 relations, DR=18.7%) show comparable violation rates despite 14× ontology size difference — with constraint tightness as the predictor — is non-obvious. The Evaluate-for regression (+5.8pp under schema-informed prompting) concretely demonstrates prompt-level unreliability.

**S2: Clean and informative ablation design.** The 5-way ablation (unconstrained / grammar-only / semantic-only / full S1 / full S2) cleanly isolates each layer's contribution. The enabling dependency finding — grammar-only barely changes DR (15.4%→14.8%), semantic-only achieves 24% reduction, but the combination reaches 94% — is well-demonstrated with sound mechanistic explanation. Grammar-only DR *increase* on DocRED (18.5%→26.2%) is a particularly informative result.

**S3: Commendable transparency.** The paper honestly reports: CF elevation to 9.9–12.0%, S2 failing to solve CF, post-hoc filtering achieving higher F1, DocRED scalability gap, and parse failure increases. This disclosure level is rare.

**S4: Cross-model validation with mechanistic explanation.** The 2×2 matrix (2 models × 2 datasets) with the dual-factor model (tightness × RV baseline) explaining Qwen DR↓45% vs Llama DR↓90% on the same ontology is analytically insightful.

**S5: Bootstrap significance testing with honest framing.** Per-dataset significance reporting (SciERC: +0.13pp, p=0.58; DocRED: +0.50pp, p<0.001) with mechanistic attribution is methodologically correct.

**S6: Post-hoc baseline comparison is multi-dimensional.** The comparison across recall, information coverage, and entity-type residuals is legitimate, not just F1.

**W1 [Major]: "Near-complete" title claim not supported by DocRED results.** Qwen DocRED retains 10.2% residual DR — more than 1 in 10 triples still violates domain/range constraints. Combined with CF=2.6%, ~13% of triples have some violation. The title is defensible for SciERC (0.93% residual) and Llama-DocRED (2.55%), but misleading for Qwen-DocRED. The paper's own dual-factor explanation makes clear effectiveness is highly contingent on model-specific vocabulary compliance.

**W2 [Major]: CF trade-off is substantial and severity distinction lacks empirical validation.** CF rises from 0.08% to 9.9% on SciERC (Qwen) and to 12.0% on DocRED (Llama). The paper frames DR as "hard" and CF as "soft," but this distinction is entirely unvalidated — no downstream experiment demonstrates CF violations are less harmful. The monotonic increase across enforcement aggressiveness (unconstrained 0.08% → semantic-only 2.71% → full S1 9.90%) suggests this is a systematic consequence that will worsen with more constraints.

**W3 [Major]: Evaluation operates at ~8% R-F1 — practical value unclear.** At ~8% R-F1, ~92% of extracted triples are incorrect. Constraints primarily operate on *wrong* triples — ensuring ontological well-formedness of factually incorrect extractions. No experiment validates whether violation rates transfer to the higher-F1 regime (fine-tuned models), or whether the dual-factor model's predictions hold there.

**W4 [Moderate]: Fallback rate / residual DR near-identity may be tautological.** The near-identity between fallback rate (10.2%) and residual DR (10.21%) on DocRED may be a mathematical consequence of system design rather than an empirical finding — if every fallback event implies a DR violation, the relationship is definitional.

**W5 [Moderate]: Limited technical novelty — domain transfer of code-generation constrained decoding.** The core mechanism (compiling type constraints into token-level logit masks with a stateful processor) transfers techniques from code generation (PICARD, Synchromesh). IE ontology constraints (flat domain/range sets over 6 entity types) are structurally simpler than what prior systems handle. The entity registry is a dictionary; mask composition is bitwise AND.

**W6 [Moderate]: Semantic-only worsens ET violations on DocRED (2.5%→4.2%).** This negative interaction — partial constraint application increasing a different violation type — is reported but underexplored. Practitioners cannot safely deploy the semantic layer alone.

**W7 [Minor]: Tightness-violation correlation on SciERC rests on 7 data points.** DocRED's 96 relations would provide far stronger evidence; the full tightness-DR scatter for DocRED is not reported.

**W8 [Minor]: Parse failure increase not well-analyzed.** Llama-DocRED parse failures increase 6.8%→9.1% under constraints. Since failures are excluded from F1/violation calculations, this creates potential selection bias.

1. Is the fallback→DR relationship definitional or empirical? What fraction of fallback events do NOT produce DR violations?
2. Have you estimated violation rates for fine-tuned IE systems? If fine-tuned models already have low DR, the practical motivation narrows.
3. What mechanism causes semantic-only to increase ET violations on DocRED?
4. Have you checked gold-standard type consistency for the dominant CF conflict patterns (Generic↔OtherScientificTerm)?
5. Why not evaluate a combined OntoCoDec + post-hoc approach?

- **Two models only** (Qwen3-8B, Llama-3.1-8B) — both 8B parameter, open-weight. No proprietary models, no larger models, no fine-tuned models.
- **Two datasets only** (SciERC, DocRED) — one small/simple, one large/complex. No mid-range ontology.
- **Zero-shot only** — the interaction between constraint enforcement and few-shot/fine-tuned extraction quality is an open question explicitly acknowledged but not explored.
- **Low-F1 regime** (R-F1 ≈ 2–8%) — constraint violations may matter less when extraction quality is already very low. The §5.6 discussion ("even small absolute F1 changes are non-trivial relative effects") is fair but does not resolve whether the method remains useful at higher F1 levels.

### W5 [Minor]: Thin Related Work / Missing References
**R2 identified gaps**:
- **Constrained decoding**: PICARD (Scholak et al., 2021) for SQL, Synchromesh (Poesia et al., 2022), SynCode (Ugare et al., 2024) — already cited but differentiation with PICARD/Synchromesh could be sharper.
- **LLM-based IE (2024–2025)**: TANL, REBEL, GoLLIE, and more recent zero-shot IE papers are missing.
- **Neuro-symbolic constraint literature**: DeepProbLog, Semantic Loss Functions, posterior regularization — these enforce semantic constraints during neural generation and are conceptually related.
- **KG embedding type constraints**: TransE/DistMult with type constraints (Krompass et al., 2015; Jain et al., 2018) address the same problem from an embedding perspective.
- **Schema-guided dialogue**: SGD (Rastogi et al., 2020) and related work on schema-conditioned generation.

**R1 concurs** that 9 references is unusually thin for EMNLP. Even accounting for page limits, the related work section should engage with at least 15–20 references.

---

## Points of Reviewer Divergence

### D1: Overall Recommendation
- **R1** (3.5): Leans toward borderline accept based on the strong ablation design, the violation landscape contribution, and the transparent analysis. Views the framework as a solid engineering contribution with the enabling dependency as a non-trivial insight.
- **R2** (3.0): Leans toward Findings based on limited technical novelty. Views the primary contribution as the empirical landscape study, with the framework as enabling infrastructure.
- **Resolution**: Consensus at **3.0 (Findings)**. The empirical contributions are solid but the novelty profile fits Findings better than main conference. With a stronger related work section and CF resolution, the paper could move to 3.5.

### D2: Decidability Taxonomy
- **R1**: Useful organizational framework, slightly overstated as a "contribution."
- **R2**: Restates obvious properties of autoregressive generation; not a standalone contribution.
- **Resolution**: The taxonomy is *useful exposition* but should not be framed as a primary contribution. It provides a principled boundary for what constrained decoding can and cannot enforce, which has pedagogical value.

---

## Questions for Authors

1. **CF severity validation**: Can you provide evidence that CF-violating triples are actually usable in downstream KG population? What fraction of CF instances represent genuine type ambiguity (where both types are defensible) vs. clear errors?

2. **Latent DR hypothesis**: For the DocRED grammar-only DR *increase* (18.46%→26.17%), can you trace a sample of grammar-corrected triples to show that OOV relation names were indeed hiding DR violations? This would strengthen the dual-factor claim considerably.

3. **Constraint Coverage predictive power**: You report CC≈89% (SciERC) and CC≈43% (DocRED). Can CC be computed *before* running the full pipeline (from the grammar alone + a small calibration set)? If so, this becomes a genuinely useful pre-deployment diagnostic.

4. **F1 regime sensitivity**: Have you considered running OntoCoDec on a few-shot or instruction-tuned model to test whether constraint enforcement effects persist at higher F1 levels? Even a small experiment (e.g., 5-shot on SciERC) would significantly strengthen the paper.

5. **Post-hoc F1 advantage**: Post-hoc filtering achieves higher F1 than OntoCoDec (Table 8). Can you clarify why — is it because post-hoc also removes CF-violating triples that happen to be false positives, giving it a precision advantage that OntoCoDec's streaming approach cannot match?

6. **Tightness-violation correlation**: The correlation between tightness and DR rate on SciERC is based on only 5–7 data points (relations). Have you tested whether this holds on DocRED's 96 relations? A scatter plot with 96 points would be far more convincing than one with 7.

---

## Recommendations for Revision

1. **Title**: "Near-Complete" is misleading given DocRED results (10.21% residual DR, Qwen) and CF rates (up to 12%). Consider: "Toward Type-Valid Information Extraction via Compiled Ontology Constraints" or keep "under Single-Relation Scope" but add "with Model-Dependent Effectiveness."

2. **CF analysis**: Add a net violation analysis — total violations before (DR+RV+ET) vs. after (residual DR + CF). Show that the net violation count decreases even accounting for CF. Validate the severity distinction with a downstream evaluation or at least a manual annotation of CF instances.

3. **Related work**: Expand to at least 15–20 references. Add PICARD, Synchromesh, TANL/REBEL, recent 2024–2025 zero-shot IE papers, and neuro-symbolic constraint enforcement literature. Sharpen differentiation: what makes IE ontology constraints harder than SQL/code constraints?

4. **DocRED evidence**: Add a triple-level tracing analysis for the latent DR hypothesis (sample 50–100 grammar-corrected triples, show before/after). This would convert the dual-factor explanation from "plausible" to "empirically validated."

5. **Tightness correlation**: Show the scatter plot on DocRED (96 relations) in addition to SciERC. If the correlation holds at scale, this substantially strengthens the landscape study. If it doesn't hold, discuss why (confounds: relation frequency, entity type distribution).

6. **Reframe contributions**: Position the violation landscape study as the primary novel contribution, with OntoCoDec as a demonstration that these violations are addressable via constrained decoding. This framing better matches the actual novelty profile.

---

## Final Assessment

This paper makes a genuine empirical contribution through its violation landscape study, demonstrating that ontology constraint violations in LLM-based IE are systematic, tightness-driven, and not reliably addressable via prompting alone. The OntoCoDec framework is technically sound and the ablation design is exemplary in its thoroughness and honesty. However, the framework's technical novelty is moderate (domain transfer of constrained decoding), the CF trade-off (up to 12%) is a significant unresolved limitation, and the DocRED results show model-dependent effectiveness that complicates generality claims. The paper is below the threshold for EMNLP main conference but is a solid candidate for the **Findings** track, contingent on addressing the thin related work section and providing stronger CF analysis.

**Consensus recommendation: Overall 3.0 — Findings acceptance.**

\subsection{Cross-Dataset Validation on DocRED}
\label{sec:docred-results}

Table~\ref{tab:docred-ablation} presents the four-way ablation on DocRED, a document-level RE benchmark with 96 Wikidata relation types---14$\times$ the ontology size of SciERC.

\end{table}

% exp_ids: phase2_docred_unconstrained, phase2_docred_full_s1
\paragraph{Core result.}
Full S1 reduces DR from 18.46\% to 10.21\% ($\downarrow$45\%), eliminates ET (2.48\%\,$\to$\,0\%), and near-eliminates RV (29.66\%\,$\to$\,0.03\%).
Relation F1 improves from 7.74 to 8.23 ($+$0.50\,pp; bootstrap 95\% CI [$+$0.23, $+$0.81], $p < 0.001$), attributable to grammar-layer elimination of 5{,}189 OOV relation predictions counted as false positives.
CF increases modestly (0.10\%\,$\to$\,2.57\%), lower than SciERC's 9.90\%.

% exp_ids: phase2_docred_grammar_only
\paragraph{Grammar layer surfaces latent violations.}
Grammar-only constraints eliminate RV and ET but \emph{increase} DR from 18.46\% to 26.17\% ($+$42\%).
This counter-intuitive result has a structural explanation: the unconstrained baseline's 29.66\% OOV relation triples cannot be evaluated for DR (no schema entry exists); grammar enforcement assigns these triples valid relation names whose domain/range rules the associated entity types frequently violate.
The grammar layer thus \emph{reveals} latent type incompatibilities, directly motivating the semantic layer.

% exp_ids: phase2_docred_semantic_only, phase2_docred_full_s1
\paragraph{Enabling dependency.}
Semantic-only constraints reduce DR by only 25\% (18.46\%\,$\to$\,13.84\%) while failing to eliminate RV (29.87\%) or ET (4.22\%).
Full S1 achieves a further 26\% relative reduction over semantic-only (13.84\%\,$\to$\,10.21\%), replicating the enabling dependency from SciERC: without grammar-enforced vocabulary, the semantic layer encounters OOV relation types for which no domain/range rules exist.

% exp_ids: phase2_docred_full_s1, llama_docred_full_s1
\paragraph{Constraint tightness governs enforcement ceiling.}
The residual DR on DocRED (10.21\%) exceeds SciERC (0.93\%) due to per-relation \emph{constraint tightness}: DocRED relations average 5.68 valid type pairs ($\bar{\tau}{=}0.842$) vs.\ 24 on SciERC ($\bar{\tau}{=}0.333$).
Tighter constraints produce narrower grammar$\cap$semantic mask intersections, increasing fallback frequency---the aggregate fallback rate (10.2\%; 1{,}770/17{,}341 triples) closely tracks residual DR (10.21\%), confirming a near-bijection between fallback events and residual violations.
Crucially, tightness interacts with the model's baseline violation profile: Qwen's high RV (29.66\%) causes grammar enforcement to surface many latent DR violations, yielding 10.21\% residual DR; Llama's lower RV (16.03\%) limits this surfacing, achieving 2.55\% residual ($\downarrow$90.2\%) on the same ontology (\S\ref{sec:cross-model}).
This dual-factor mechanism---tightness $\times$ baseline RV---explains cross-dataset and cross-model DR reduction differences.
